topic: Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth while its data link is down
why_selected: Strongest verified story in the window: NASA primary source plus independent reporting; awe, a live twist, highly visual, global.
research_summary: NASA's Voyager blog (18 Nov 2026) says the mission will confirm on Thursday 19 November that Voyager 1 is operating one light-day from Earth, about 25.9 billion km, making it the first spacecraft to get that far. On 14 November the team noticed it had stopped sending science and engineering data; a Deep Space Network antenna in Canberra still hears its carrier signal, which suggests the probe is pointed at Earth and its radio works. NASA says the missing data points to the onboard computer that collects and formats data, and that with a one-way delay of about 24 hours diagnosis may take weeks or longer. Independent outlets report the same. The exact crossing time was not confirmed from a primary page, so the script says this week.
key_facts: One light-day: about 25.9 billion km (16.1 billion miles).
No science or engineering data since 14 Nov; carrier signal still received.
NASA suspects the data-formatting onboard computer; diagnosis may take weeks.
uncertainties: Exact time of the crossing not confirmed from a primary page.
Cause of the data loss not yet known.
context: Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in 2012. A similar onboard-computer fault in 2023-24 was eventually fixed.
script:
A message to Voyager 1 now takes a full day to arrive.

This week it became the first spacecraft one light-day from Earth. That's about 25.9 billion kilometres away.

But here's the part most people missed. Since November 14, it has sent back no science data at all.

NASA can still hear its carrier signal, so it seems to be pointed at Earth and working. NASA suspects the computer that packages its data.

And every command takes a day to get there, and another day for an answer.

So a machine launched in 1977 is being fixed from farther away than anything we've ever built.
